A flue is a channel — a hollow passage — through which smoke, hot gases, steam, or hot air travels from a source of heat to the outside world. Think of it as a dedicated escape route for heat and harmful gases produced by burning something.
The Most Common Use: Inside a Chimney

This is where you'll encounter the word most often.

When you light a fire in a fireplace, or when a furnace or boiler burns fuel, it produces smoke and dangerous gases like carbon monoxide. These cannot be allowed to fill the room. They need to travel upward and exit the building. The passage inside the chimney through which all of this travels is the flue.

Here's an important distinction many people miss: the chimney and the flue are not the same thing. The chimney is the physical structure — the brick or stone tower you see on a rooftop. The flue is the hollow channel running inside that chimney. The chimney is the body; the flue is the throat.

In fact, a single chimney can contain multiple flues — one connected to the fireplace on the ground floor, another connected to a furnace in the basement, for example. Each is a separate passage, even though they share the same outer structure.

The flue works because of a simple physical principle: hot air and gases are lighter than cool air, so they naturally rise. This rising movement creates a draft — a continuous pull that draws smoke upward through the flue and out of the building, while also drawing fresh air toward the fire to keep it burning.

Understanding these related terms will make your knowledge complete:

  • Flue liner: The inner lining of the flue — often made from clay tiles, ceramic, or metal. It protects the surrounding chimney structure from heat and corrosive gases, and prevents dangerous gases from seeping through cracks into the building.
  • Flue damper (or just damper): A movable plate or valve inside the flue that you can open or close. When the fireplace is in use, you open the damper to let smoke escape. When the fireplace is not in use, you close it to stop cold outdoor air from drafting back down into your home.
  • Flue gas: The mixture of gases — including carbon dioxide, water vapor, and traces of carbon monoxide — that result from burning fuel and travel out through the flue.

Flues appear in an industrial and engineering context too. Inside a fire-tube boiler (a type of boiler used to heat water and produce steam), there are metal tubes called flues. Hot gases from burning fuel pass through these tubes, and the water surrounds the outside of them. The heat transfers from the gases inside the flues to the water outside, turning it into steam. Here the flue is not a chimney passage but a heat-exchange tube — yet the concept is the same: a channel through which hot gases travel.

There is a secondary, more specialized use of this word in music. In a pipe organ, pipes are divided into two families: reed pipes (which make sound using a vibrating metal reed) and flue pipes (which make sound differently). In a flue pipe, a thin, precise stream of air is directed through a narrow slot — called the flue — and across a sharp lip. This causes the air column inside the pipe to vibrate and produce a tone, much like the sound you produce when you blow across the opening of a bottle. The flue here is that small, carefully shaped slot or opening in the pipe's foot.

For completeness, two older uses exist but are seldom encountered today:

  • Flue as fluff or fiber: In older English, "flue" could mean soft, downy fibers — like the fluff that comes off wool, fabric, or feathers. You are very unlikely to see this in modern writing.
  • Flue as a fishing net: A wide-mouthed net used for catching fish. This is essentially obsolete.

Flue is frequently confused with flu (short for influenza, the illness). They sound identical but mean completely different things. The word with the silent e at the end — flue — always refers to the channel or passage.
A flue is a channel or passage — most commonly found inside a chimney — designed to safely carry smoke, combustion gases, or hot air away from a heat source and out of a building or system.
